class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>It’s difficult to summarize Williams’ role in the creation of “To Leave You” and its kin with a one-word job title such as “choreographer. In assembling artists of several stripes and guiding their creativity with her prompts, she could be called a director, engineer or even a conductor.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Barry Brecheisen/For the Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Williams often finds nontraditional dance venues, entertaining even a Chinese restaurant for “To Leave You.” She landed on Three Top Lounge at the Salt Shed, responding to some alchemy of the decor, the views and the openness. "There was just something that I was like, 'Oh, this is the place,'" she said.</p><p>In developing “To Leave You,” Williams and the other artists followed paths that presented themselves to them. Similarly, “To Leave You” itself was a path that appeared after Williams’ two most recent pieces. “Echo Mine” was inspired by the dancer Claire Bataille, who became ill and passed away before the piece premiered. Then “Hisako’s House” explored the legacy Williams’ grandmother left her, and was performed on-site in her grandmother’s house in Lombard. Hisako, too, died before the premiere. The meditations on mortality that arose from those two artistically entwined deaths sparked “To Leave You.”</p><p>At the lounge inside the Salt Shed, the audience will move around as the performance unfolds, promenade-style. “Like stepping into the world from the get-go, with us,” Williams said. Another boundary made permeable. Who knows what future works will emerge from the embers of this one?</p>

entries.title: "Once Upon a Time in Harlem" documentary introduces audiences to Chicago journalist Gerri Major
entries.summary: <p>At the height of the Harlem Renaissance in the 1920s, the city bustled with activity.</p><p>People recited Langston Hughes’ “Weary Blues” poem on street corners. Duke Ellington delivered electrifying performances at the Cotton Club. A'Lelia Walker, daughter of millionaire Madam C. J. Walker, drew an enviable guest list to salons at her townhouse.</p><p>There to capture it all was Gerri Major, a glamorous journalist and Chicago native whose columns covered the Black upper class until her death at 90 years old in 1984. Nicknamed the “Harlem hostess,” she wrote for several newspapers before becoming a senior editor at Ebony and the society editor at Jet magazine.</p><p>Major is a central figure in “Once Upon a Time in Harlem,” William and David Greaves’ critically acclaimed documentary playing in select Chicago theaters in November. The film, featured in the <a class="Link" href="https://web.saic.edu/blackharvestfest/" target="_blank" ><u>Black Harvest Film Festival</u></a> running Nov. 6-15 at the School of the Art Institute of Chicago’s Gene Siskel Film Center, captures a party attended by Major, composer Eubie Blake, painter Aaron Douglas and more than 20 other Harlem Renaissance luminaries at Duke Ellington’s home in 1972.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-050000" name="image-050000"></a> <picture class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>In “Once Upon a Time in Harlem,” Gerri Major describes herself as a “helpful” journalist to the Black community. “If I had a choice of saying something that would hurt our people or keeping quiet, I would keep quiet.” </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Carl Van Vechten Papers/Beinecke Rare Book and Manuscript Library</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Major’s body of work is a detailed chronicle of Black life, history and genealogy, but she has remained an obscure figure — until now.</p><p>“She was an important journalist in terms of just raising the profile of what was happening with the people during that time,” said Liani Greaves, who is David’s daughter and one of the documentary’s producers. “The purpose of our film is to tell those stories to insert the renaissance into the cultural memory of the nation.”</p><p>Also a fashion icon, Major has <a class="Link" href="https://nmaahc.si.edu/explore/collection/search?edan_q=%2A%3A%2A&edan_fq%5B%5D=name%3A%22Major%2C%2BGerri%22&op=Search" target="_blank" ><u>a dress</u></a> featured in the National Museum of African American History and Culture’s collection. She is a regal presence in “Once Upon a Time in Harlem,” adorned in gold necklaces and bracelets and green rings that match her flower-patterned dress. In the documentary, she converses warmly with the other guests, including other Chicago natives: librarian Regina Andrews, historian Nathan Huggins and activist Louise Patterson.</p><p>Major also reminisces about throwing her own lavish parties at her home on West 139th Street, the cultural mecca known as “Strivers’ Row,” as well as her career.</p><p>She describes herself as a “helpful journalist” rather than a “great journalist.”</p><p>“If I had a choice of saying something that would hurt our people or keeping quiet, I would keep quiet,” she says in the film. “If I couldn’t do something that was going to give us a boost up, I was never going to give us a boost down.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>In 1953, Gerri Major joined the staff of magazines Ebony and Jet, covering major events such as the coronation of Queen Elizabeth II in England. She is pictured here in 1972 in a still from “Once Upon a Time in Harlem.”</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Courtesy of Neon</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Born Geraldyn Hodges in 1894, her exposure to Black socialites began in her childhood in the Douglas community area. She was given a debutante ball at 18 and earned a bachelor’s degree in philosophy at the University of Chicago. But her early life wasn’t without struggle, especially as one of few Black women at the college.</p><p>“We were humiliated and put down and crucified, but we stuck it out,” she says in the film.</p><p>Before moving to Harlem, she married Dr. Henry Binga Dismond, the first of her three husbands, and taught at Stephen A. Douglas Elementary School. She also participated on a commission to investigate the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-history/2025/11/08/chicago-race-riot-1919-memorial-loop" target="_blank" ><u>Chicago Race Riot of 1919</u></a>.</p><p>Besides reporting for the New York Amsterdam News, Pittsburgh Courier and other outlets, she worked as a publicist, radio announcer and writer with New York’s public health department.</p><p>In 1953, she joined the staff of magazines Ebony and Jet, owned by the Chicago-based Johnson Publishing Company. She traveled frequently, covering the coronation of Queen Elizabeth II in England, writing about a dictator in the Dominican Republic and overseeing the company’s Paris bureau. Her column for Jet, “Gerri Major’s Society World,” ran until her death.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a the 1976 book, “Black Society,” tracing the evolution of the Black upper class from the 1700s to contemporary times.</p><p>William Greaves initially sat on the “Once Upon a Time in Harlem” footage while continuing to shoot more content about the renaissance. After he died in 2014, his family worked to restore and release the film.</p><p>David Greaves, William's son, said it was important to share the stories of Major and others in the documentary at a time when Black history is being removed from schools and other institutions.</p><p>Seeing the film is “an act of resistance,” he added.</p><p>Major also felt her life was a lesson for younger generations.</p><p>“They have to remember that there are those of us who are now old, who have struggled, and worked hard, and had little to work with, had little sympathy, had no civil rights, had nothing, and we struggled and went ahead and worked and some of us died doing it,” she says in the film.</p><p>“And if they cross us all off, they’ve lost a great thing.”</p><p><i>Contributing: Justine Tobiasz</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-e20000" name="module-e20000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><b>Where Chicago audiences can see “Once Upon a Time in Harlem” </b><br><br><b>Music Box Theatre </b><br>Beginning Nov. 9<br>3733 N. entries.title: Flock, maker of controversial license plate readers, starts to give campaign cash to local politicians
entries.summary: <p>Flock Safety license plate reading cameras have spread throughout the Chicago area, stirring controversy about surveillance and civil liberties while helping snare crooks.</p><p>The company’s money has also begun to spread to local politics, according to election records.</p><p>In Cicero, where Flock has a number of cameras monitoring traffic, the Atlanta company has given several campaign contributions to Town President Larry Dominick, who oversees public safety in the near west suburb.</p><p>The first contribution to the Cicero Voters Alliance (The Larry Dominick Team) was for $1,000, made in 2021, according to Illinois State Board of Elections records.</p><p>In 2022 another $1,000 arrived from Flock, while in 2024 the company gave $2,000.</p><p>In 2025, the year Dominick successfully ran for reelection, Flock gave him another $2,000.</p><p>The community now has 31 Flock cameras, and first engaged the company in or about 2020, a town spokesman said.</p><p>“The Town of Cicero is proud of the hundreds of crimes solved with the help of Flock cameras and our officers would be utilizing them to help keep the community safe with or without the $6,000 they’ve contributed to President Dominick over the last six years,” the spokesman said.</p><p>Dominick appears to be the only local municipal leader to have received Flock campaign cash so far. But the company did donate to two candidates for sheriff in the collar counties.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a technology.</p><p>Idleburg handily won reelection on Tuesday against Buchberger.</p><p>Flock officials didn’t respond to requests for comment.</p><p>Records show Flock employs two firms to lobby on its behalf in Illinois, including Cozen O’Connor Public Strategies, which is affiliated with a Philadelphia law firm and appears to have been hired by Flock in early 2024.</p><p>Since then, the company has given around $485,000 in campaign money to state and local candidates and political causes, according to elections board records that show employees or consultants of Cozen O’Connor gave an additional $14,000 during the same time frame.</p><p>Cozen O’Connor also represents several dozen other clients in Illinois, from the rideshare company Lyft to Planned Parenthood of Illinois and <a >Catholic Charities</a>, Starbucks and the YMCA of Metropolitan Chicago, state records show.</p><p>National Strategies LLC, which is based in Washington, D.C., and serves as another Flock lobbying firm in Illinois, didn’t report any donations to state or local campaign accounts, though members of the business have donated to numerous federal campaigns.</p><p>As <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2026/10/15/lobbyists-campaign-contributions-juliana-stratton-us-senate-general-election" target="_blank" >the Chicago Sun-Times has reported</a>, Flock has used the bipartisan firm Mercury Public Affairs for federal lobbying, and members of the firm have given campaign money to — and participated in a campaign fundraiser for — Juliana Stratton in her run for U.S. Senate.</p><p>Flock CEO Garrett Langley gave a $1,000 contribution in 2024 to a campaign fund benefiting U.S. Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.) target="_blank" >Fran Spielman</a></h5><p><b>North Side tragedy</b>: A fire tore through a Rogers Park townhome early Thursday, killing a family of four, including a 13-year-old, and their dog, officials said.</p><p><b>The victims</b>: The boy was identified as 8th-grader Valentino Vallejo in an email to families from his school. pandemic, the Jan. 6, 2021 insurrection, the Supreme Court's decision to strike down Roe v. Wade, the 2023 mayoral election, the 2024 Democratic National Convention, Operation Midway Blitz and much more.</p><p>Simons became the host of WBEZ's morning news and talk show "In the Loop" in September 2025 and is the only Chicago journalist with a regular sit-down with Mayor Brandon Johnson, the monthly series "Ask The Mayor."</p><p>"Leading 'Reset' and now 'In the Loop' has been one of the great privileges of my career," Simons said. "I am truly thankful for the Chicagoans who welcomed me into their lives and trusted me with their stories, questions and hopes for this city. obscurity in acclaimed documentary</a></h3><p></p><h5>Reporting by <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-yddukykt-l-th/" target="_blank" >Erica Thompson</a></h5><p>At the height of the Harlem Renaissance in the 1920s, the city bustled with activity.</p><p>There to capture it all was Gerri Major, a glamorous journalist and Chicago native whose columns covered the Black upper class until her death at 90 years old in 1984. Nicknamed the "Harlem hostess," she wrote for several newspapers before becoming a senior editor at Ebony and the society editor at Jet magazine.</p><p>Major is a central figure in "Once Upon a Time in Harlem," William and David Greaves’ critically acclaimed documentary playing in select Chicago theaters in November.</p><p>The film, featured in the <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-yddukykt-l-tk/" target="_blank" >Black Harvest Film Festival</a> that's running Friday through Nov. 15 at the School of the Gene Siskel Film Center, captures a party attended by Major, composer Eubie Blake, painter Aaron Douglas and more than 20 other Harlem Renaissance luminaries at Duke Ellington's home in 1972.</p><p>Born Geraldyn Hodges in 1894, her exposure to Black socialites began in her childhood in the Douglas community area. She was given a debutante ball at 18 and earned a bachelor's degree in philosophy at the University of Chicago.</p><p>Major's body of work is a detailed chronicle of Black life, history and genealogy, but she has remained an obscure figure — until now.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-yddukykt-l-tu/" target="_blank" ><b>READ MORE</b></a></p><hr><p></p><h4>YOUR DAILY QUESTION ☕️</h4><p>Yesterday, we asked you: <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-yddukykt-l-ir/" target="_blank" >After Tuesday’s nationwide wins, what is your message to Democrats as they prepare to take control of the House and Senate?</a></p><p>Here’s some of what you said, edited for length and clarity:</p><p>"Don't f--- it up. Take care of your constituents, work with your colleagues in Congress, be decent. The best reelection campaign is a good record." — <i>Phoebe M.</i></p><p>"Affordability and accountability. You don’t have to choose one over the other. Do both." — <i>Thomas Rodriguez</i></p><p>"Small standalone bills that 70% of the country wants. Oversight, keep the borders tight but get rid of ICE inside our country, stop the war, forget impeachment you don't have the votes, [lower] drug prices and fix the insurance nightmare." — <i>Caryn Seidman</i></p><p>"Focus on governing. Put investigations on the back burner. Forget about impeachments. Pass dozens of single-topic clean bills that force Republicans to vote on each issue and then, if passed, force Trump to sign or veto. Implement the things that are needed to make the lives of ordinary Americans better. Deliver actual results." — <i>Usha Gupta</i></p><p>"People want results. Don’t think that Texas and Kansas suddenly became California. People didn’t become MAGA two years ago, and they’re not DSA now. The pendulum will keep swinging until someone gets it right." — <i>John Paul</i></p><hr><p></p><h4>PICTURE CHICAGO 📸</h4><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" entries.title: Electric scooter driver, 67, killed in collision with speeding SUV in North Park
entries.summary: <p>In the second fatal electric scooter crash in as many days, a 67-year-old man scooter driver has died after a collision with a speeding SUV early Friday in the North Park neighborhood on the Northwest Side. </p><p>The stand-up scooter driver, an unidentified 67-year-old man, was in the intersection of the 3300 block of West Peterson Avenue around 4:35 a.m. when a Dodge SUV "made contact" with him, Chicago police said. </p><p>He was taken to Saint Francis Hospital in Evanston where he was pronounced dead, police said. </p><p>The Dodge driver was cited for speeding.</p><p>Another electric scooter driver was<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/11/05/electric-scooter-driver-dead-after-collision-with-cpd-vehicle-in-bridgeport" target="_blank" > killed in a crash</a> early Thursday after a collision with a Chicago police vehicle in Bridgeport. </p><p>In that accident, officers were on patrol in a marked police vehicle, traveling north on Princeton Avenue where they “came into contact” with a stand-up electric scooter operated by a 39-year-old male at 32nd Street, police said in a statement.</p><p>The still-unidentified scooter operator suffered injuries to his body and was taken to Stroger Hospital, where he was pronounced dead, police said.</p>

entries.title: Man facing attempted murder charges after shooting boy, 17, in Gresham police say
entries.summary: <p>A man is due in court Friday accused of shooting a 17-year-old boy in Gresham earlier this week. </p><p>Dennis Cain, 32, was arrested several hours after the Tuesday shooting and charged with attempted murder, aggravated battery, aggravated assault and possessing a weapon as a felon, Chicago police said. </p><p>Cain, of the 8600 block of South Muskegon Avenue, allegedly unlawfully entered a home around 12:50 a.m. Tuesday in the 7700 block of South Lowe Avenue and shot the teen in the back, police said. </p><p>A 12-year-old was also in the home at the home but wasn't hurt. </p><p>Cain was expected to appear in court Friday. </p>

entries.title: 3 shot when bullets smash through window of Englewood apartment
entries.summary: <p>Gunfire ripped through an apartment window and hit three people inside the Englewood apartment early Friday on the South Side,</p><p>Two women, 21 and 23, were inside an apartment when the shooting happened around 1:10 a.m. in the 400 block of West Marquette Road, Chicago police said. </p><p>They were both shot in the legs and were taken to the University of Chicago Medical Center where they were in fair condition, police said. </p><p>A 21-year-old man was shot in the chest and took himself to the Little Company of Mary Hospital where he was in good condition, officials said. </p><p>Area 1 detectives were investigating. </p>

entries.title: Why Tyler Bertuzzi's goal-scoring has disappeared for Blackhawks this season
entries.summary: <p>TAMPA, Fla. — When the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks" target="_blank" >Blackhawks</a> set higher expectations for the 2026-27 season, they were counting on most of their established players repeating their 2025-26 performances and some up-and-coming players taking big steps forward.</p><p>The latter has happened. Touted rookie forwards Roman Kantserov and Anton Frondell and enigmatic second-year defenseman Artyom Levshunov have been three bright spots.</p><p>The former, however, has not happened across the board. Spencer Knight's save percentage has dropped from .902 to .892, and his analytics depict an exactly league-average goalie so far. Patrick Kane hasn't scored since the season opener — but had taken seven minor penalties between then and getting injured Monday.</p><p>And Tyler Bertuzzi, who led the Hawks with 32 goals last season, is stuck on just two goals this season — one of which was an empty-netter.</p><p>"Sometimes they go in, sometimes they don't," Bertuzzi said recently. "I feel like I haven't been able to get as many grade-A chances, and then some games I'm getting a lot of chances. If you're getting chances, that's a good thing. Eventually they'll go in. [You] just have to keep creating chances. I'm looking for those spots to get open."</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Tyler Bertuzzi has uncharacteristically missed some tap-ins this season, like this one against the Kings: <a href="https://t.co/JvvXDHuaHP">pic.twitter.com/JvvXDHuaHP</a></p>— Ben Pope’s Video Clips (@BenPopeCSTclips) <a href="https://x.com/BenPopeCSTclips/status/2118585502609691056?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">November 6, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>The 31-year-old winger seems like a particularly poor fit in coach Jeff Blashill's high-pressure system, which is designed to take advantage of the Hawks' team speed.</p><p>That speed is prevalent in most of their young forwards (and on-the-way prospects). But Bertuzzi, on the other hand, is one of the NHL's slowest skaters.</p><p>In the Hawks' aggressive 2-1-2 forecheck, the puck is often gone before he gets low enough to pressure opposing defensemen, and then he's caught chasing the play back up the ice.</p><p>TNT panelist Paul Bissonnette <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/11/04/blackhawks-panthers-tnt-paul-bissonnette-connor-bedard" >ripped</a> Bertuzzi for a poor forecheck during the first period Wednesday against the Panthers, but a more effective Bertuzzi forecheck did help create Roman Kantserov's second-period goal. Bertuzzi later said he thinks the Hawks' forecheck has improved recently.</p><p>"Our [defensemen] are down the walls a lot more, and we're keeping pucks alive," Bertuzzi added. "Sometimes we can get a little bit in-between. We've got to be fast-paced, just on top of everyone."</p><p>The fact most of the Hawks' scarce offense comes off the rush rather than from offensive-zone cycles — plus that most of their cycle chances are one-and-done because they struggle to retrieve loose pucks — particularly hurts Bertuzzi, too.</p><p>He's one of the league's most efficient finishers around the net, but that relies on teammates getting the puck to the net. If they don't, the so-called "human backboard" isn't as useful.</p><p>During five-on-five play, Bertuzzi is averaging just 6.5 shot attempts per 60 minutes, down from 10.7 last season. And on the power play, he's averaging 10.8 attempts per 60, down from 18.6. He was taken off the top power-play unit this week for the first time all season.</p><p>"We've got to do a better job of getting more pucks...for him to get opportunities for rebound looks, tip looks, things like that," Blashill said recently. "That's not on him; that's on our team. Right now, we're just not generating enough across the board."</p><p>Even when the Hawks do generate close-in chances for Bertuzzi, he isn't finishing them at his usual rate. Only 47.2% of his attempts have made it successfully on-goal (down from 55.4% last season) and only 5.5% have gone in (down from 10.8%).</p><p>Bad luck is a contributing factor, and that should balance out over time, even if the systemic issues will take more effort to resolve. He has had several should-have-been tap-ins shockingly skitter wide in recent games.</p><p>"It just needs to cross the red line," he said. "I'll keep going to the net. I'm not too worried about it."</p>
